question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example that is normally quoted for a tonic – v
opening in the Beatles catalogue is the i – v start of Eleanor Rigby in
E minor.

The verse/string intro is in E minor and the music is set up on the tonic
E minor and is immediately answered by the diatonic fifth degree of the
mode, B minor, the v chord of E minor / the minor fifth-degree chord of
the related major.  In the key the move is the familiar I → v, tonic to
the minor fifth-degree triad, a perfect-fifth root jump which gives the
song its open, slightly hollow entry.  The same I → v, tonic-to-minor-
fifth idea is the one that is usually illustrated in the rock-theory
literature with the big E-major → B-minor opening of Helter Skelter /
the G-major opening of A Hard Day’s Night, the latter being the pop
 shorthand for the I → v / tonic-to-the-minor-fifth-chord jump that the
question is after.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Penny Lane

The opening of Penny Lane is the clear example I’m hearing. The track is in A major and the first two bars are built around a very deliberate tonic-to-minor-fifth jump: a full A major tonic chord is stated on the downbeat, and it is immediately answered by an E minor chord, the minor v. That A → Em motion sets up the whole piccolo trumpet fanfare and the light, almost music-hall quality of the intro, and you can hear the jump right at the start before the verses kick in. It’s the same kind of stark fifth-relationship lift that defines the early Sgt. Pepper side of the catalogue, and on first listen the A major to E minor opening is unmistakable as the signature chord jump.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Penny Lane – The piccolo trumpet fanfare that opens the track is in D major, the song’s tonic, and the first sustained harmonic support under the vocal entry is A minor, the minor v of D. That tonic-to-minor-fifth jump, D to A minor, is the bittersweet lift you hear right at the start of the verse and is the harmonic signature most people remember from the opening.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: A Day in the Life. The opening is built around that stark A major tonic that hangs for a beat before the harmony drops straight to the E♭ minor triad, the chord built on the minor fifth of A. It’s that tritone jump that gives the first statement its disorienting, almost cinematic shock, and it’s first heard in full in the piano intro before the orchestra comes in. The effect is the same tonic-to-minor-fifth leap that defines the song’s unsettled opening mood.

15.text:
The jump that the textbooks always point to is the I – v / i – v
opening that the group used over and over in 1964-65.

In G major the opening guitar figure of A Hard Day’s Night is
articulated as

  G  –  E m  –  G …

in other words tonic G major to the diatonic fifth-degree triad E minor,
v in G major, i.e. a perfect-fifth/root movement tonic → the minor fifth
chord. It is the same I→v motion that is heard in the same way in the
E major / B minor opening of Help! and in the E minor / B minor i→v
ostinato that opens Eleanor Rigby, the minor-mode version of the
familiar Beatles tonic-to-minor-fifth jump.

The G–Em opening is the one normally quoted for A Hard Day’s Night,
the classic I–v tonic-to-minor-fifth jump. The same class of opening is
heard on Help! – E major to B minor – and on Eleanor Rigby – E minor to
B minor – in the minor-mode form i→v.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The classic example that is normally quoted is the opening of *A Hard Day’s Night*.

The number is in G major. The very first two harmonies that are heard under the vocal entry are

* I  = G major – the tonic
* v  = D minor – the fifth degree of G major taken with the minor quality

In root-position spelling that is the tonic G major jumping up a perfect 5th to the
minorised dominant / v, G → D minor, a I – v move. In the familiar recording the
first G is the famous ‘G with an added 4th’ G–B–D–G–C sonority and the next
harmonic area the band lands on is D minor, the minor fifth of the tonic.

The same I – v jump is the one that is usually illustrated in the key of E
major, e.g. the opening of *Helter Skelter*, E major → B minor, E the tonic and
Bm the minor fifth/v of E major. That E → Bm opening is the E–major analogue
of the G → Dm opening of *A Hard Day’s Night* and is the textbook Beatles I→v
‘tonic to minor fifth’ jump.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is usually cited for that tritone / I → bV effect is the 1969 Abbey Road opener Come Together.

The riff is normally heard in C and the first harmonic gesture is the tonic C being set up and then immediately juxtaposed with the chord a tritone away, Gb ≈ F♯, the flat-five / minor-fifth of the tonic. In functional terms the first two harmonic areas heard are I → bV, i.e. the tonic area jumping to the chord built a minor fifth / tritone above the tonic. It is that I – bV jump, often described in pop writing as the tonic to the minor-fifth/flat-fifth chord, that gives the song its famously unsettled, bluesy opening and which is the Beatles’ most quoted tritone opening.

That is the gesture that is normally taught as “Come Together’s tonic to flat-five / minor-fifth jump”. If the I → v reading is wanted strictly as the diatonic minor fifth degree, the same family of openings is the one normally illustrated by the Abbey Road opener.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The jump that is normally quoted in this connection is the opening
tritone / I – v-type opening of **Come Together**.

In the recording the intro is heard in the home area of E with the very
characteristic E-major “tonic” hammered on the guitar / bass and then the
line is answered by the chord / pitch a diminished / minor fifth above it,
the bV / v area B♭  –  in functional terms the v of the song’s A-major
centric area, the minor dominant E – Bm in band discussion.  It is the
I → v / I → ♭V leap that gives the famous Come Together opening its
unresolved, blues-rock bite and it is the Beatles’ textbook example of a
tonic-to-minor-fifth launch.

The same I → v move is the one that is most often quoted in the more
literal I–v sense for the early Beatles repertoire, e.g. the A-major → E-
minor opening of Strawberry Fields Forever, A major tonic jumping down a
perfect fifth to its minor dominant v, the classic tonic-to-minor-fifth
jump that is the model for the Come Together opening.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The most often quoted example in this family is the 1966
A-minor string piece **Eleanor Rigby**.

The verse is in A natural minor and it is presented with the
characteristic minor-key i – v opening. The first sounding harmony
is the A-minor tonic

    Am  = i

and the music immediately jumps to the chord built on the 5th degree
of the A natural minor scale, the v chord

    Em = v

i.e. the minor “fifth” chord of the key. In root terms A → E is the
perfect 5th above the tonic and in A minor the fifth degree is
minor, hence the tonic–minor-fifth i–v jump that opens the song.
The same i–v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening is the one most commonly
quoted for the E-major / B-minor opening of *Norwegian Wood*,
E = I → Bm = v, which is the major-mode illustration of the same
idea.

4.text:
In the Parlophone / Revolver era the most often quoted textbook example of an
I – v opening is the piano introduction to

*She’s Leaving Home* – and the same I – v lay-out is the one that is normally
cited for the Penny Lane / Eleanor Rigby family of openings.

In the song’s home key the introduction is written in A major.
The first big piano chord is the tonic

    A – major  = I

and the second harmony that the vocal line is put on is the fifth degree
in its minor quality

    E – minor = v

A – E is a perfect fourth up in the bass, i.e. a tonic-to-the-minor-fifth
chord jump, and the v is left hanging, wanting to resolve to i in the
relative minor, which is exactly the unsettled colour that characterises the
opening of the ballad.  The same I–v lay-out is the one that is normally
taught with the Bb-major Penny Lane intro, Bb major  →  G minor, the
tonic of the song moving a fourth up to its minor fifth degree, and it is
that v-colour that is heard on the very first two bars of Eleanor Rigby in
E minor, Em → Bm.

9.text:
The textbook Beatles “tonic → tritone’’ opening is the one that is quoted
over and over again for *I Am the Walrus*.

In the normal F–major reading the piece comes in on a big F-major
tonic and immediately falls to the flat-five minor triad Db-minor,
F  →  Dbm, i.e. I → bV, a root movement of a diminished / minor 5th,
the tritone.  It is that F → Dbm jump that is normally pointed to as the
Beatles’ classic tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone kick-off, the
same kind of I–bV shock that is most famously associated in the popular
literature with the G–Db side of the famous “A Hard Day’s Night’’ opening.
That is the opening that is usually demonstrated as the I–v / I–bV
tonic-to-minor-fifth jump in The Beatles’ catalogue.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The jump you are thinking of is the I – v / I – ♭V leap that the Beatles
put at the very front of a number of their early numbers.

In the literal I–v sense the textbook example is And I Love Her.  The
verse is in A major and the song is opened by a big A-major tonic
strum which is immediately answered by the v-chord E-minor, i.e. the
minor chord built on the 5th degree of the scale, a perfect-fifth
tonic-to-fifth jump which is heard in the record as a tonic → minor-fifth
chord leap.  The same I→v opening is the one that is normally quoted
for I Saw Her Standing There / All My Loving etc.

That is the jump that is normally cited in the literature as the Beatles’
famous opening chord jump.  The more extreme tritone tonic → ♭V jump
that is often spoken of in the same breath is the E–B♭ tonic-to-minor-fifth
/tritone opening of Helter Skelter / I Am the Walrus, the E-major tonic
being answered immediately by the flat-fifth B♭ major chord, the
classic Beatles I→♭V tritone leap.  A Hard Day’s Night is the popular
name that is attached to the whole family of Beatles opening leaps.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about an opening tonic → minor-fifth-degree chord jump, i.e. I → v in major or i → v in minor, a perfect-fifth root movement to a minor-quality fifth-degree triad. Colleagues are giving many of the same family of Beatles openings and disagreeing on key/detail and on whether the jump is diatonic v or the tritone flat-V reading.

Most cited family:
* A Hard Day’s Night in G major. Several colleagues give G → D minor as the I → v launch, the textbook G-major example; a minority give G → E minor for the same song. This is repeatedly called the classic textbook Beatles I → v opening.
* And I Love Her / Help! / I Saw Her Standing There / Please Please Me etc. in A major: A major tonic → E minor v, i.e. I → v a perfect fifth down. Colleague 10 flags And I Love Her A → E m as the literal I–v textbook example.
* Helter Skelter / Norwegian Wood in E major: E major → B minor v, the E-major analogue of the A → E m move. Colleague 12 and 15 cite this.
* Eleanor Rigby in E minor / A natural minor. Multiple colleagues give Em → Bm, or Am → Em, i → v in minor, the minor-mode version of the same idea. Colleague 1, 2 and 15 present this as the i–v example.
* Penny Lane is offered in D major → A minor by colleague 13 and in A major → E minor by colleague 7, showing key confusion around the same I → v idea.
* Come Together / Helter Skelter / A Day in the Life / I Am the Walrus are repeatedly brought in by some colleagues under a tritone / I → ♭V reading, e.g. E → B♭/Gb, A → E♭, F → D♭m. That is a tonic-to-flat-five / minor-fifth-interval tritone leap, not the diatonic v move the wording seems to ask for, though it is conflated in the discussion.

Disagreements noted:
* Exact chord for A Hard Day’s Night: G → D minor vs G → E minor vs the famous G-add4 sonority.
* Whether the intended interval is diatonic v or the tritone flat-V. Colleagues 5, 11, 14, 9 explicitly move to I → ♭V/tritone examples Come Together, A Day in the Life, I Am the Walrus.
* Key centre for Penny Lane and Come Together shifts across responses.

Current belief: the diatonic I → v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening is a well-known 1964-65 Beatles device. The most frequently named canonical instance in the thread is A Hard Day’s Night, with Helter Skelter E → Bm and Eleanor Rigby Em → Bm / Am → Em as the clearest unambiguous minor-mode i → v examples. And I Love Her A → Em is also a widely quoted literal I → v launch. Unresolved is which specific song the question setter intends among this family and whether they meant the diatonic v or the tritone flat-V reading that several colleagues are conflating with “minor fifth”.

4.text:

1.text:
The textbook pop-theory example that is always quoted for a Beatles tonic → minor fifth-degree launch is the opening of *A Hard Day’s Night*.

In G major the number is launched on the tonic and the first vocal entrance is put on the diatonic fifth degree taken in its minor quality, the v of the key. In root terms that is the familiar

 G  →  D minor

I → v, tonic to the minor fifth-degree triad, a perfect-fifth root jump. The famous G-add4 opening sonority G–B–D–G–C is heard as the tonic and the harmony is immediately answered by the minorised dominant/D-minor area that underlies the first vocal phrase. The same I→v tonic-to-minor-fifth family is the one that is routinely illustrated with the A-major → E-minor opening of And I Love Her / Help! / I Saw Her Standing There / She’s Leaving Home / While My Guitar Gently Weeps and with the minor-mode i→v ostinato of Eleanor Rigby in E minor → B minor / A minor → E minor, and in E-major form with Helter Skelter / Norwegian Wood E → Bm.

That is the diatonic I→v jump the literature means by “tonic to the minor fifth chord”. The same language is often used loosely for the tritone I→♭V shock that is most famously associated with Come Together / I Am the Walrus, e.g. E → B♭ / F → D♭m, which is the I→♭V version of the tonic-to-a-minor-fifth-interval idea.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The example that is actually taught as the Beatles’ textbook tonic-to-minor-fifth launch is the opening of *A Hard Day’s Night*.

The number is in G major. What you hear at the very first vocal entrance is the famous G major sonority, the G–B–D–G–C voicing that people call the “A Hard Day’s Night chord”, i.e. the tonic I, followed immediately by a landing on D minor. D is the 5th degree of G major and the chord is used in its diatonic minor quality, D–F–A, the v of G major. Root-wise that is G up a perfect fifth to D, a clean I → v tonic-to-minor-fifth jump, not a tritone and not a major V.

That is why the opening is quoted in the literature as the prototypical I→v Beatles move. The E major → B minor analogue is the same class of motion, and it is that G → Dm realisation that people remember from the record. The confusion with G → Em comes from hearing the E in the bass of the famous added-4th voicing, but the harmonic area the band actually settles on for the first two beats of the verse is D minor, the minor fifth degree of the tonic.

Come Together, A Day in the Life, I Am the Walrus are I – bV / I – ♭V moves, a diminished/minor fifth tritone, which is a different colour from the diatonic perfect-fifth I – v move. That's useful to separate, because a lot of the discussion is conflating the two.

I think the clearest textbook case in the catalogue for a literal tonic → v, perfect-fifth root jump, is the opening of A Hard Day's Night, and it's the example most of the rock-theory literature actually uses.

The song is in G major. The first thing you hear under the vocal entry is the famous G with an added 4th sonority, G-B-D-G-C, which is the tonic area, and it lands immediately on D minor. G → D is a perfect fifth up in the bass, and D minor is the diatonic v of G major, the minor chord built on the fifth degree. That's the I – v tonic-to-minor-fifth jump the question is after, and you can hear it as a clean root-position fifth movement, not as a tritone.

That's why the same I – v family gets illustrated in E major as E → Bm, the Helter Skelter opening, and why it's so often quoted alongside the I – v openings in Help!, And I Love Her, While My Guitar Gently Weeps, etc. It's the same gestural family, just transposed.

I agree with the point being made about the tritone confusion. Come Together, A Day in the Life, I Am the Walrus are I – bV / I – ♭V moves, a diminished/minor fifth tritone, which is a different colour from the diatonic perfect-fifth I – v move. That's useful to separate, because a lot of the discussion is conflating the two.

On the Strawberry Fields Forever mention, I think that's exactly the kind of shorthand that gets repeated for the whole I – v family. The Mellotron-spliced intro is famously a bit of a collage and is often misremembered as a clean A → Em tonic jump. In the actual recording the harmonic rhythm is more melodic and phased, which is why the clean textbook example people point to is the G → Dm opening of A Hard Day's Night rather than Strawberry Fields.

In the pop-theory shorthand that move is conventionally named for

*A Hard Day’s Night*.

The number is in G major. The first harmonic area heard under the vocal entry is the tonic, the famous G-add4 / G-sus sonority G–B–D–G–C, i.e. I, and it is answered immediately by the diatonic fifth degree of G major taken in its minor quality, D minor, the v of the key. This is distinct from the loose pop-writing “tonic to a minor-fifth interval’’ = I→♭V tritone family Come Together E→B♭, I Am the Walrus F→D♭m, A Day in the Life A→E♭m.

The I→v / i→v family is real and widespread 1964-66. In major the cleanest unarguable textbook instances are A = I → E minor = v: And I Love Her, Help!, I Saw Her Standing There, She’s Leaving Home, While My Guitar Gently Weeps; and the E-major analogue E = I → B minor = v: Norwegian Wood, Helter Skelter.

In minor the move is i→v and is transcriptionally unambiguous: Eleanor Rigby E natural minor string intro/verse ostinato Em = i → Bm = v, E→B perfect fifth, B minor the diatonic fifth degree of E natural minor in minor quality; same colour in A-natural-minor spelling Am = i → Em = v.

A Hard Day’s Night is the pop-theory shorthand the literature compresses the whole I→v family into, conventionally cited as G = I → D minor = v, the famous G-add4/G-sus tonic answered by the minorised fifth degree. The name is attached to the family, but the second harmony under the first vocal entrance is actively contested in the round: colleagues 6,10,13,15 and others hear/analyse it as D major = V or G→Em = vi, making G→Dm a pedagogical idealisation rather than a clean recording. Colleagues 1,7,11,14 defend G→Dm as the intended move. That dispute is why Eleanor Rigby Em→Bm i→v and And I Love Her A→Em I→v remain the least disputed, verifiably clean textbook instances.

Strawberry Fields Forever is repeatedly misremembered as a clean A→Em jump; the Mellotron-spliced intro is a collage and not a clean textbook tonic→v launch.

Unresolved: which single song the question intends. If canonical shorthand is required, the literature points to A Hard Day’s Night G→Dm with the caveat of the chord-quality dispute. If strict diatonic verifiability is required, Eleanor Rigby Em→Bm i→v is the cleanest, with And I Love Her A→Em I→v as the clean major-mode analogue. I still need precise verification of the first two sounding harmonies for A Hard Day’s Night G→? to resolve popular name vs verifiable example tension.

Strictly diatonic “tonic to the minor fifth-degree triad’’ = a perfect-fifth root move I→v in major / i→v in minor, tonic to the diatonic fifth degree taken with its minor quality. That is a different class from the loose pop-writing “tonic a minor fifth / tritone away’’ I→♭V family Come Together E→B♭, I Am the Walrus F→D♭m, A Day in the Life A→E♭m.

On the strict diatonic v reading the 1964-66 family is real.

* Major mode I→v. The verifiably clean textbook instance is And I Love Her A = I → E minor = v, A→E a perfect fifth, the same A→Em layout that is heard in Help!/ I Saw Her Standing There / She’s Leaving Home / While My Guitar Gently Weeps and the E-major analogue E = I → Bm = v in Norwegian Wood / Helter Skelter.
* Minor mode i→v. The transcriptionally uncontested realisation is Eleanor Rigby. E natural minor / A natural minor, string intro/verse ostinato Em = i → Bm = v, E→B a perfect fifth, B minor the diatonic fifth degree of E natural minor in minor quality. In A-natural-minor spelling Am = i → Em = v. It is the literal tonic→minor fifth-degree triad launch with no voicing dispute.

A Hard Day’s Night G = I → D minor = v is the pop-theory shorthand the literature compresses the whole I→v / i→v family into, the famous G-add4/G-sus tonic answered by the minorised fifth degree. That is why the name persists for the family. The G-major opening is now the disputed member of the set: the harmony that settles under the first vocal entrance is routinely heard/analysed as D major = V or G→Em = vi, so the G→Dm citation is best treated as a pedagogical idealisation of the family rather than a clean transcription.

So for a strict, verifiably clean diatonic tonic → minor fifth-degree v chord the least disputed recording is Eleanor Rigby Em→Bm i→v, with And I Love Her A→Em I→v as the cleanest major-mode analogue. If the question is being used in the popular shorthand sense in which the whole I→v family is named, the name that the literature attaches to the class is A Hard Day’s Night.

I’m staying with the strict diatonic reading and keeping the two families separate.

Diatonic “tonic to the minor fifth degree” = a perfect-fifth root move I → v in major and i → v in minor, tonic to the diatonic 5th degree taken with its minor quality. That is a different colour from the loose pop-writing “tonic a minor fifth/tritone away” I → ♭V family Come Together E → B♭, I Am the Walrus F → D♭m, A Day in the Life A → E♭m.

On the strict I → v / i → v reading the 1964-66 Beatles house move is real. The literature compresses the whole family under the popular shorthand *A Hard Day’s Night*, conventionally quoted as
G = I → D minor = v,
the famous G-add4/Gsus tonic answered by the minorised fifth degree. That is the same gestural class as
A = I → E minor = v in *And I Love Her / Help! / I Saw Her Standing There / She’s Leaving Home / While My Guitar Gently Weeps* and
E = I → B minor = v in *Norwegian Wood / Helter Skelter*.

The G-major opening is the most contested member of the set. The harmony that settles under the first vocal entrance is routinely heard/analysed as D major = V or G → Em = vi, so the G → Dm citation is best treated as a pedagogical idealisation of the family.

Once the name is separated from the move the move itself is transcriptionally unambiguous. The least disputed, analysis-independent realisation of a literal tonic → minor fifth-degree triad is the minor-mode ostinato:

*Eleanor Rigby* – E natural minor / A natural minor
Em = i → Bm = v
E → B is a perfect fifth root movement and B minor is the diatonic fifth degree of E natural minor taken in its minor quality. In A-natural-minor spelling the same i → v colour is Am = i → Em = v.

*And I Love Her* A = I → E minor = v is the cleanest unarguable major-mode analogue of the same perfect-fifth I → v jump, heard on the first two bars before the vocal.

For a verifiably clean, transcription-independent recording of a strict diatonic tonic → minor fifth-degree v chord I will vote *Eleanor Rigby* Em → Bm i → v, with *And I Love Her* A → Em I → v as the clearest major-mode counterpart. *A Hard Day’s Night* remains the popular name the literature attaches to the whole I → v family.

I think the diatonic vs intervallic split is what actually settles this.

Once you keep the loose pop-writing I→♭V tritone family Come Together E→B♭, I Am the Walrus F→D♭m, A Day in the Life A→E♭m strictly separate, what remains is the perfect-fifth root move I→v in major and i→v in minor, tonic to the diatonic fifth degree taken with its minor quality. That is the 1964-66 house gesture the literature means by “tonic to the minor fifth degree chord”.

A Hard Day’s Night is the popular name the rock-theory literature puts on the whole family, conventionally quoted as G=I→D minor=v with the famous G-add4/Gsus tonic. That shorthand is useful as a family label, but the recording is the messiest member to defend here. The harmony that settles under the first vocal entrance is routinely heard as D major I→V and the G→Em reading sometimes quoted is vi not v, which is why Colleague 6, 10, 13 and others are flagging it as a pedagogical idealisation.

That dispute is exactly why we need a transcriptionally unambiguous exemplar. In minor mode the move is clean and uncontested:

Eleanor Rigby is in E natural minor / A natural minor and the string intro/verse is a two-chord ostinato Em = i → Bm = v. E→B is a perfect-fifth root movement and B minor is the diatonic fifth degree of E natural minor taken in its minor quality. In A-natural-minor spelling it is Am = i → Em = v. It is the literal tonic → minor fifth-degree triad launch with no voicing dispute.

And I Love Her A = I → E minor = v is the cleanest unarguable major-mode analogue of the same perfect-fifth I→v jump, the same layout you hear in Help!/I Saw Her Standing There/She’s Leaving Home/While My Guitar Gently Weeps and E = I → Bm = v in Norwegian Wood/Helter Skelter.

That is why Strawberry Fields Forever keeps getting mentioned and then withdrawn. The Mellotron-spliced intro is a collage and is commonly misremembered as a clean A→Em jump. The harmonic rhythm is phased and it is not the uncontested perfect-fifth tonic→v launch people are looking for. It is shorthand that gets repeated for the whole I→v family but it is not the clean textbook case.

So for a strict, verifiable diatonic tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree v chord the least disputed recording is Eleanor Rigby Em→Bm i→v, with And I Love Her A→Em I→v as the clear major-mode counterpart. A Hard Day’s Night remains the conventional name attached to the whole I→v/i→v family.
